body.text: As the contest for the next Secretary-General of the UN gets into gear, the focus is once again on the future of the world body. Dag Hammarskjöld, the second Secretary-General of the UN, had famously said, “The UN was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell,” expressing, hopefully, that humanity’s highest aspiration should be for peace rather than victory.

The UN today has not been capable of achieving peace. It has also become a huge, bloated bureaucracy, with an alphabet soup of overlapping development organisations and ineffective peacekeeping operations. The Security Council, its main organ for peace, is no longer representative of the global distribution of economic and military power. It needs major reform, alongside other UN organisations.

The UN’s predecessor, the League of Nations, had collapsed because the US did not join it, and Japan and Germany withdrew from it after being reprimanded for declaring war, while Italy’s attack on Abyssinia (present-day Ethiopia) was not reprimanded. Today, we again see unilateral wars initiated by major powers—Russia against Ukraine and the US against Iran—but they have not been condemned by the Security Council as both countries have veto powers to block any such condemnation. The US, which has been very critical of the UN’s ineffectiveness and its position on climate change and migration, is not withdrawing from the UN but is now pushing for major reforms within it.

The UN80 Initiative, a reform programme, is under way and is expected to save over $500 million, largely by moving jobs from headquarters to the field, and through better coordination of facilities. But this would barely scrape the surface of what is needed. The reforms ambit includes a “Humanitarian Overview”, which has deliberately lowered targets, and hyper-focussing resources strictly on saving 87 million lives in immediate jeopardy in five countries—Afghanistan, Haiti, Palestine, Somalia, and Sudan. This has left broader, long-term community resilience and structural support to development banks and alternative financing mechanisms. Success even with these more limited objectives will require more than just humanitarian relief coordination.

On the development side, many new UN organisations were created over the last 20 years—including the United Nations Population Fund, United Nations Women, and the United Nations Office for Project Services—that were carved out of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), with very high overheads. A United Nations Environment Agency was created with many duplicate functions with the UNDP. The UN country teams and regional teams now spend an enormous amount of time and energy just on coordination of these agencies. One UN official described it as “herding cats”. All these development-related agencies, which were hived off to suit some donor country’s interest, could be consolidated into a single development agency.

Similarly, it is not clear why the world needs three trade organisations (the WTO, United Nations Commission for Trade and Development, and the International Trade Centre, all based in Geneva), and three food-related organisations (the Food and Agriculture Organization or FAO, the World Food Program, and the International Fund for Agricultural Development, all based in Rome). There are two organisations for migration (International Organization for Migration and the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, both based in Geneva). Merging them into one each for trade, food and agriculture, and migration would result in huge savings.

Then there are huge bloated regional commissions which serve like a UN headquarters for the respective regions of the world (the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, and the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia). These should be staffed with experts who can help UN country teams deliver better technical advice to the country, helping them focus on developmental priorities. But they are instead busy organising regional conferences and preparing reports, some of which are useful but many are not.

The UN has come up with a very broad developmental agenda called the “Sustainable Development Goals”, which was agreed to by all member countries in 2015, with 17 goals and a staggering 169 targets. But instead of helping countries decide on priority areas based on their current stages of development so that they can make the best use of their limited resources, UN agencies have a tendency to try to work on all of them in each country. This pursuit of a vast global agenda in every country for every goal and target results in the wastage of resources and dilution of effectiveness.

Climate change is among the biggest threats humanity faces this century. UN climate change reports have highlighted the dangers and sounded increasingly urgent warnings. A Conference of the Parties (COP) is held every year to take forward the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change agenda on climate action, signed in 1992 and endorsed by the Paris Agreement in 2015. But with the US walking out of the agreement twice, and with funding cuts, progress has been slow, as was evident at the COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year.

Although there was some progress on methane finance, adaptation funding, and carbon market rules and transparency, the outcome was inadequate, leaving the world off track as far as the goals for 2030 were concerned. The final decision that was adopted did not mention fossil fuels, omitted a coal/oil/gas phase-out roadmap, and offered only soft language on adaptation finance. With potential funding cuts of up to 40 per cent, climate-vulnerable countries are left facing intensifying storms, floods, and droughts largely on their own. Ironically, oil price shocks due to the Iran war may end up doing more to shift the world to renewables than all the COPs put together.

While armed conflict is at a long-term high, political and financial support for UN peacekeeping operations has reached a new low. These developments are not surprising at a time when international cooperation has increasingly given way to nationalist policies and populist rhetoric. There have been some failures, but many studies show that UN peacekeeping is effective in protecting civilians, preventing civil war recurrence, reducing death tolls, containing violence, and limiting refugee flows. Moreover, the prospect of UN peacekeeping eventually facilitates peace settlements.

By turn, the next Secretary-General of the UN must be from Latin America, and there is clamour that it be a woman. Given the abysmal state of the UN, it is important that the person be prepared for the more serious and cutting-edge reforms. Perhaps someone not already in the UN would be better suited to carry out radical surgical reforms that the organisation badly needs. It is often said that the job pertains more to that of a “secretary” than a “general” because those who have tried to be like a “general” have been undermined by the big powers, especially the US. The joke around the UN is that the current incumbent, the former Prime Minister of Portugal, António Guterres, is neither “secretary” nor “general” and has done very little for world peace. He focussed recently on Cyprus while wars raged in Ukraine, Iran, and Sudan, and, not to mention, with the ongoing conflict and lawlessness in Congo and Haiti.

India has had no clear strategy for getting the best out of the UN system. China, for example, has strategically managed to place people in key positions of its interest, such as at the WHO, at the FAO, and as Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs. The US had always had an American heading the World Food Programme and UNICEF and as the Under-Secretary-General for Political Affairs. The UK always has a Brit heading the Humanitarian Coordinator position, and the French, the Under-Secretary-General of Peace Operations position.

Indians have held senior positions in the UN but by their own merit and not by any strategic push from the country. India could and should have used its contributions to influence positions such as the heads of the World Intellectual Property Organization and the WHO, given the stature of its pharmaceutical and IT industries, but it has not done so. Indian troops have in the past played a key role in peacekeeping operations. India can and should also try to play a key role in managing or influencing peacekeeping operations and not just be a troop contributor.

India’s long-standing goal is to get a permanent seat at the Security Council. So, any Secretary-General candidate who is for an expansion of the permanent members of the Council would be suitable. But India’s aspirations for that reform may, nevertheless, have to wait. India remains 6th in world GDP rankings, behind the US, China, Germany, Japan, and the UK, and is only likely to get ahead of the three latter countries by 2030. India is also punching below its weight in world affairs, while countries like Pakistan and Türkiye are more active and are playing the peacemaker’s role. India needs to be seen as a significant contributor to peace and progress and not just as a bystander focussed on safeguarding only its own interests. India must further repair relations in its own neighborhood to be taken more seriously by others.

Whether the UN will be able to recover from its current crisis remains to be seen. What is certainly needed is a well-respected and functioning UN to stop the world from going to hell. Let us hope a more dynamic Secretary-General can lift the game.
